results.text:
AMD Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)

# AMD Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

 November 03, 2026 4:15 pm EST Download as PDF 

AMD delivers record quarter as Data Center segment revenue grows 97% year-over-year, driven by record sales of AMD Instinct GPUs and AMD EPYC CPUs

SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) today announced financial results for the third quarter of 2026. Third quarter revenue was $13.4 billion, gross margin was 54%, operating income was $2.8 billion, net income was $2.4 billion and diluted earnings per share was $1.46. On a non-GAAP (*) basis, gross margin was 56%, operating income was $3.9 billion, net income was $3.5 billion and diluted earnings per share was $2.09.

“We delivered a record quarter with revenue exceeding the high end of our guidance as Data Center segment sales nearly doubled year-over-year,” said Dr. Lisa Su, AMD chair and CEO. “Demand for our Instinct and EPYC products continued to strengthen, and we expect growth to accelerate further in the fourth quarter as we scale Helios and ‘Venice’ production. With our leadership product portfolio and deep customer and supply chain relationships, we are confident in our ability to sustain very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years.”

“Third quarter revenue grew 45% year-over-year to a record $13.4 billion, while non-GAAP earnings per share grew 74%, demonstrating the significant operating leverage in our business model as our Data Center business drives scale,” said Jean Hu, AMD executive vice president, chief financial officer and treasurer. “Our fourth-quarter outlook reflects accelerating revenue and earnings growth, driven by strong demand across our Data Center portfolio.”

GAAP Quarterly Financial Results

| | Q3'26 | Q3'25 | Y/Y | Q2'26 | Q/Q |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Revenue ($M) | $13,377 | $9,246 | Up 45% | $11,536 | Up 16% |
| Gross profit ($M) | $7,210 | $4,780 | Up 51% | $6,203 | Up 16% |
| Gross margin | 54% | 52% | Up 2 ppts | 54% | Flat |
| Operating expenses ($M) | $4,378 | $3,510 | Up 25% | $4,213 | Up 4% |
| Operating income ($M) | $2,832 | $1,270 | Up 123% | $1,990 | Up 42% |
| Operating margin | 21% | 14% | Up 7 ppts | 17% | Up 4 ppts |
| Net income ($M) | $2,428 | $1,243 | Up 95% | $2,297 | Up 6% |
| Diluted earnings per share | $1.46 | $0.75 | Up 95% | $1.38 | Up 6% |

Non-GAAP(*) Quarterly Financial Results 

| | Q3'26 | Q3'25 | Y/Y | Q2'26 | Q/Q |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Revenue ($M) | $13,377 | $9,246 | Up 45% | $11,536 | Up 16% |
| Gross profit ($M) | $7,483 | $4,992 | Up 50% | $6,488 | Up 15% |
| Gross margin | 56% | 54% | Up 2 ppts | 56% | Flat |
| Operating expenses ($M) | $3,560 | $2,754 | Up 29% | $3,394 | Up 5% |
| Operating income ($M) | $3,923 | $2,238 | Up 75% | $3,094 | Up 27% |
| Operating margin | 29% | 24% | Up 5 ppts | 27% | Up 2 ppts |
| Net income ($M) | $3,471 | $1,965 | Up 77% | $2,760 | Up 26% |
| Diluted earnings per share | $2.09 | $1.20 | Up 74% | $1.66 | Up 26% |

Segment Summary

- Data Center segment revenue was a record $8.5 billion, up 97% year-over-year, driven by strong demand for AMD EPYC™ processors and the launch of AMD Instinct™ MI450 Series GPUs. 
- Client and Gaming segment revenue was $3.7 billion, down 8% year-over-year. Client business revenue was $2.9 billion, up 7% year-over-year, driven by sales of AMD Ryzen™ mobile processors. Gaming business revenue was $773 million, down 40% year-over-year, due to lower semi-custom and graphics revenue.
- Embedded segment revenue was $1.1 billion, up 29% year-over-year, led by growth in aerospace and defense, automotive, communications and industrial end markets. 

Recent Highlights 

- AMD solutions and software are powering superintelligence infrastructure at scale: 

- Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are running models and workloads on the first AMD Helios™ rackscale solutions, powered by AMD Instinct MI450 Series GPUs and 6 th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs.
- HPE announced that Vultr will deploy the first AMD Helios by HPE systems.
- Oracle Cloud Infrastructure announced its OCI Compute E7 cloud compute instances will be powered by 6 th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs, supporting enterprise applications and the CPU services surrounding models.
- AMD introduced the AMD Helion reference architecture, an open, flexible blueprint for building rack-scale agentic systems that lets customers configure the mix of CPUs and GPUs based on their workloads.
- AMD ROCm™ 10 was released, bringing AI-native developer experiences to AMD platforms with ROCm.AI, along with performance improvements and updated libraries, compilers, frameworks, tools and model support.
- The EuroHPC JU selected AMD Instinct MI430X GPUs and 6 th Gen AMD EPYC processors to power the LUMI-AI supercomputer.
- Google Cloud and Microsoft announced general availability of storage-optimized cloud

# Earnings Call: Q3 2026

Nov 3, 2026

 Summary

Q3 set records for revenue and operating income, led by Data Center, while Client and Gaming weakened. Management expects >80% revenue growth in 2027, with supply constraints and a declining PC market among key risks.

Operator

 Welcome to the AMD third quarter 2026 conference call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance during the conference, please press star zero on your telephone keypad. Please note that this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Matt Ramsay, VP Financial Strategy and IR. Thank you, Matt. You may begin.

Matt Ramsay

VP of Financial Strategy and Investor Relations, AMD

 Thank you, and welcome to AMD's third quarter 2026 financial results conference call. Lisa Su

results.author: Daragh Thomas
results.text:
AMD's AI Data Center Guarantees Reach $8.5 Billion as It Challenges Nvidia
# AMD's AI Data Center Guarantees Reach $8.5 Billion as It Challenges Nvidia
Daragh Thomas Wed, November 4, 2026 at 12:54 PM EST 3 min read
## Trading disclosure
The above button links to Coinbase. Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational.
**Advanced Micro Devices Inc.** (NASDAQ: AMD) is taking on billions of dollars in potential financial obligations to help customers build AI data centers, as it steps up its challenge to **Nvidia Corp.** (NASDAQ: NVDA).
AMD's lease guarantees jumped 88% in just three months, from $4.1 billion in June to $7.7 billion in September. Another $750 million in debt guarantees brings the total potential exposure to approximately $8.5 billion.
If its partners run into financial trouble, AMD could be on the hook for as much as $8.5 billion.
AMD has also signed another $13.3 billion in data-center leases that haven't started yet. It plans to pass the facilities on to partners, but could still be left paying the rent if those partners can't.
### Why AMD Is Backing Data Centers
AMD is helping customers secure data centers where its chips can be installed, potentially generating billions in future sales.
On Tuesday's earnings call, Bank of America analyst **Vivek Arya** questioned whether customers had sufficient financing, land and power to support roughly 3 gigawatts of planned AMD deployments in 2027.
CEO **Lisa Su** said AMD was working closely with customers to prepare infrastructure years in advance.
"We know where the GPUs are going in terms of which data centers and which locations," Su said, adding that AMD was being "selective and strategic" about investing alongside partners.
A July deal with **Core Scientific Inc**. (NASDAQ: CORZ) shows how AMD is helping create a market for its own chips.
Core Scientific agreed to provide data-center capacity for 529 megawatts of computing. AMD leased 377 megawatts itself and provided financial backing for a cloud provider taking the remaining 152 megawatts.
That helps secure the facilities where AMD's processors can be deployed, but also leaves the chipmaker exposed if its partners cannot pay.
And there's a potential reward beyond chip sales. AMD received warrants to buy up to 30 million Core Scientific shares at $23.47 each, with its rights increasing as more capacity is leased.
### Nvidia Is Playing the Same Game
Nvidia is pursuing a similar strategy on a much larger scale.
Its August filing revealed $108.5 billion in potential guarantees, including $105 billion backing a massive Ohio data center leased to OpenAI.
In return, the 4.25-gigawatt campus will use Nvidia's AI hardware almost exclusively. Nvidia estimates each generation of equipment installed there could generate $150 billion to $200 billion in revenue.
The guarantees take effect in stages starting in fiscal 2029, with payments required only if OpenAI defaults.
### No Defaults So Far
AMD ended September with $15.8 billion in cash and short-term investments. No commercial partners had defaulted, and AMD had made no guarantee payments.
But the chipmaker warned that financing problems, permitting delays or partners failing to meet their obligations could force it to make payments "without realizing the anticipated economic benefits."
*Image: Shutterstock*

results.author: Matteo Parrino
results.text:
AMD Books $1.1 Billion Warrant Loss On OpenAI And Meta Deals As Its Stock Climbs

# AMD Books $1.1 Billion Warrant Loss On OpenAI And Meta Deals As Its Stock Climbs

A rising share price pushed AMD's customer warrants into a $1,097 million loss, while partner guarantees now total $8.5 billion.

#### Matteo Parrino, Jonathan Ponciano

 04 Nov 2026 — 2 min read 

AMD's 10-Q, filed Wednesday, shows the chip designer took a $1,097 million loss in the third quarter on warrants it granted to OpenAI and Meta, enough to push other income to a $902 million loss. The charge arrived next to a growing list of commitments that put AMD's balance sheet behind its customers' data center buildouts, including $8.5 billion in guarantees.

## A loss that tracks the stock

Each warrant covers up to 160 million AMD shares at an exercise price of $0.01. The company remeasures the liability each period, and the change in value lands in other income (expense), net.

That line swung to $(902) million from $82 million a year earlier. The prior quarter's 10-Q said no tranches had vested and the warrants had no effect on results.

The weighted-average fair value is now $178.58 per share, against $14.25 at grant. AMD carries a $1.2 billion warrant liability and $4.5 billion of unrecognized grant-date value, which will reduce revenue as qualifying customer sales are recorded. No warrant shares had vested or become exercisable as of September 26.

The 10-Q warns that the stock price will keep moving GAAP earnings. Past changes, it says, have produced substantial non-cash charges, and future ones may produce non-cash gains or losses.

## Operations still strong

AMD, a global semiconductor company, reported net revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% from a year earlier. Net income was $2.4 billion, against $1.2 billion. Data Center revenue rose 97% to $8.5 billion, while Gaming revenue fell 40%.

A $772 million discrete tax benefit tied to stock-based compensation also helped the quarter, and AMD booked an income tax benefit of $555 million.

## Guarantees and leases on AMD's books

The filing puts maximum gross exposure at $7.7 billion on data center lease guarantees and $750 million on partner debt guarantees, totaling $8.5 billion. As of September 26, no partner was in default and nothing had been paid. AMD would pay only on a default.

AMD also has $13.3 billion of data center leases not yet commenced that it expects to assign or sublease to partners, and $6.2 billion of cloud compute commitments. It has subleased some leases and expects $0.9 billion in sublease payments through 2036.

In August AMD issued $4.75 billion of senior notes and repaid $875 million of notes at maturity. Total debt stood at $7.1 billion, against $3.3 billion at the end of 2025. AMD also invested $1.0 billion in a public company's equity offering in October.

AMD expects its Taalas and World Labs acquisitions to close in the fourth quarter, and guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%.

The weighted-average fair value is now $178.58 per share, against $14.25 at grant. AMD carries a $1.2 billion warrant liability and $4.5 billion of unrecognized grant-date value, which will reduce revenue as qualifying customer sales are recorded. No warrant shares had vested or become exercisable as of September 26.

...

## Guarantees and leases on AMD's books

The filing puts maximum gross exposure at $7.7 billion on data center lease guarantees and $750 million on partner debt guarantees, totaling $8.5 billion. As of September 26, no partner was in default and nothing had been paid. AMD would pay only on a default.

AMD also has $13.3 billion of data center leases not yet commenced that it expects to assign or sublease to partners, and $6.2 billion of cloud compute commitments. It has subleased some leases and expects $0.9 billion in sublease payments through 2036.

results.text:
In Exchange for the Guarantees — Tessera Blog

# In Exchange for the Guarantees

Tessera's piece of 2 September held back on supplier-side residual value guarantees, saying that whether any given arrangement qualified as circular "depends on documents we have not read". The filings have now been read, and they had been on file all along. AMD disclosed a $4.1 billion guarantee of a partner's data center lease obligations in February, Nvidia disclosed guarantees of partners' facility lease obligations "in exchange for warrants" the same month, Broadcom's backstop appeared on 9 June, and Nvidia's largest guarantee in an 8-K on 17 August. Every one was public before the 2 September piece said otherwise. Checking those sources against Tessera's August work turned up errors in three pieces, corrected here and in a note on each page. They cover the date at which anyone first had to price AI hardware, four telecom figures from the Nortel and Lucent era that were wrong or unsupported, and the shape of AMD's investment in Anthropic. One argument is weaker as a result. Staging was offered as what separates today's commitments from the telecom era, and Lucent's were largely undrawn too. Revenue separates them more.

October 14, 2026 21 min read

## Key Takeaways

- · The supplier-side guarantees Tessera declined to characterize on 2 September were already on file: AMD's $4.1 billion in February, Nvidia's warrant-linked guarantees the same month, Broadcom's backstop on 9 June, and Nvidia's largest in an 8-K of 17 August.
- · Nvidia's quarterly report puts its guarantees at $108.5 billion in total, $105.0 billion of it the cap on its initial SB Energy commitment covering about 4.25 gigawatts of IT load with an OpenAI affiliate as tenant.
- · The filed form of guaranty is explicit about the exchange: the landlord agreed to the lease only if the guarantor executed it, and the premises will exclusively deploy Nvidia reference architecture for at least twenty years.
- · Three errors in Tessera's August pieces are corrected, and one August argument is weaker for it: staging was offered as what separates these commitments from the telecom era, but Lucent's were largely undrawn too, so revenue separates them more than staging does.

12 October 2026. Filings, reporting and figures are as of the dates stated in the text.

Interest disclosure: T-OpenAI and T-Kalshi are tokenized loan participation rights providing economic exposure linked to those companies' pre-IPO valuations, each issued through a dedicated issuing subsidiary. T-SpaceX, issued through its own dedicated issuing subsidiary, provides economic exposure linked to SpaceX; following the SpaceX listing, the investment underlying T-SpaceX is being divested. Redemption opens only once a Redemption Start Date is announced, and as of 12 October 2026 none has been. This piece discusses guarantees for a facility whose tenant is an OpenAI affiliate, and warrants issued to OpenAI. It also discusses Anthropic, which competes with OpenAI, so Tessera's interest in how Anthropic's financing is received does not run in one direction: a competitor's valuation sits on one side, and on the other sits SpaceX, which its prospectus records as supplying compute to Anthropic. SpaceX's quarterly report also records AI hardware it leases, so how lenders treat chip-backed credit bears on it too. No Tessera product references Anthropic, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Meta or SB Energy, and none is planned. Tessera's founder, and entities he controls, hold related exposure. Read what follows with that in mind.

Tessera's piece of 2 September, The Price of Walking Away, separated residual value guarantees into two shapes. Meta guaranteeing the residual on a campus it will occupy was, it said, "a tenant pricing its own exit". A supplier guaranteeing the residual on a facility built to house its own product was a different thing: "the guarantee underwrites demand for what the supplier sells. That is the structure The Money Goes Round, published on 28 August, examined in a different instrument."

The same piece noted that Meta's arrangement had been described as circular financing and said that "on the filing, it plainly is not." On the supplier side it held back: "Whether any given supplier-side arrangement qualifies depends on documents we have not read, and this piece does not characterize any specific one on the strength of reporting about it."

We have now read the filings, including the form of Nvidia's guaranty filed with its quarterly report. The arrangements had been on file all along. AMD's annual report, filed in February, disclosed a $4.1 billion guarantee of a commercial partner's data center lease obligations. Nvidia's annual report, filed the same month, disclosed guarantees of partners' facility lease obligations "in exchange for warrants". highlights:
The

...

## AMD: Guarantees That May Be Given for Warrants

AMD's disclosure is the least specific. Its quarterly report records "a maximum gross exposure of $4.1 billion from guarantees issued in connection with certain commercial partner data center lease obligations with terms up to 15 years." It continues: "Guarantees typically become payable in the event of a commercial partner's default and may be issued in exchange for warrants." They are carried at fair value, as a credit derivative, and were "not material to the financial statements" (10-Q, quarter ended 27 June 2026). The filing does not say what the buildings will hold.

AMD also runs warrants the other way. It issued them to OpenAI in October 2025 and to Meta in February 2026, each "to purchase up to an aggregate of 160 million shares ..." at a cent each, vesting against GPU purchases and AMD share-price targets (8-Ks and 10-Q). As of 27 June none had vested. Who Counts the Capex said of AMD: "The second interlock is genuinely circular, and it runs in both directions at once." The warrants to OpenAI and Meta were one direction, and that stands. The other direction was the Anthropic commitment, which rested on "its own cash" and "no warrants attached", both corrected above.

...

The risk, then, lies in correlation as much as in size. Nvidia's and Broadcom's guarantees, like Meta's, pay a shortfall against what the asset fetches, and AMD's filings give no formula. A tenant's guarantee can come due in bad times too, but the tenant chooses the moment, and leaves only when leaving costs less than staying. A supplier's is called by someone else's default, on a customer the supplier may already depend on for revenue.

How much that matters depends on how specific the product is to the customer, how large the customer is in the supplier's business, and why the customer defaults. If the customer fails on its own while capacity is scarce, a powered campus may re-let quickly, and Nvidia can take the lease itself. If the market broke it, the campus re-lets into that same market, and resold chips compete with new ones. The second case is where the correlation sits. Nvidia's spokesperson told Reuters, of its chip-backed financing plans, that its "AI compute is a productive, durable and fungible asset that can support long-term financing." That argument concerns chips. The Ohio guarantee covers lease and power payments on a land, power and shell buildout, so what Nvidia recovers depends on re-letting a campus for about 4.25 gigawatts of IT load in whatever market exists then. Hardware that resells can also shrink a payout without shrinking the overlap, because chips another buyer takes are chips the supplier does not sell to that buyer.
results.summary:
Summary:

- The article analyzes guarantees AMD has issued related to AI data-center leases and how these obligations could affect its risk profile.
- AMD’s disclosure indicates a maximum gross exposure of up to $4.1 billion from guarantees tied to certain commercial-partner data-center lease obligations (terms up to 15 years). These guarantees are typically payable if a partner defaults and may be issued in exchange for warrants; they are carried at fair value as a credit derivative and were not material to the financial statements (as of the June 27, 2026 quarter).
- AMD also issues warrants to partners: OpenAI (October 2025) and Meta (February 2026) to purchase up to 160 million shares in total at a nominal price, vesting based on GPU purchases and AMD share-price targets. As of June 27, none had vested. Another related commitment involving Anthropic had no warrants attached.
- The main risk is correlation risk, not just size. Guarantees from Nvidia, Broadcom, and Meta function as shortfalls if the underlying asset’s value is insufficient; AMD’s filings do not provide a clear formula for calculating potential payouts.
- The likelihood and impact depend on factors like product specificity to the customer, the customer’s size relative to AMD’s business, and the reasons for customer defaults. Two scenarios:
  - If a tenant defaults during tight capacity, the campus can be re-let or repurposed, potentially mitigating losses.
  - If a market-wide downturn occurs, re-letting competes with new chip sales, increasing payout risk.
- Nvidia’s stance that AI compute is a durable, fungible asset supports long-term financing using chip-backed guarantees, while the Ohio-based guarantee covers broader assets (land, power, shell) and depends on re-letting a large data-center capacity. Hardware resales can reduce payouts without necessarily reducing overlap with the original obligation.

Key takeaway: AMD’s data-center guarantees carry sizable exposure with correlation-driven risk, particularly in a stressed AI compute market; the OpenAI and Meta warrants add optional upside but currently do not vest, while the Anthropic arrangement lacks warrants.
